title: Bread can't sell below $8. Then what?
hook: A rule guarantees bakers a higher price. Who could lose from that?

knows: that buyers want less and sellers offer more at a higher price
the bread model where the two lines cross (supply-demand)
doesNotKnow: that a price held above where the lines cross leaves goods unsold

misconception: A higher guaranteed price helps sellers without costs.
objective: The learner can explain that a price floor above where supply and demand cross raises the price but leaves a surplus, because buyers want fewer loaves while bakers bake more: at $8 in the bread model, 20 bought, 60 baked, 40 unsold.

claims.text: In the bread model (buyers want 100 − 10p, bakers bake 10p − 20) the lines cross at $6 and 40 loaves.
With a floor at $8, buyers want 20 loaves and bakers bake 60, so 40 go unsold.
With the floor at $8 the price rises $2 and the loaves actually sold fall from 40 to 20.
A floor at or below $6 changes nothing: the market price is already at least that high.
claims.source: market(f) uses max(f, 6); for f ≤ 6 the outcome is $6, 40 loaves, 0 unsold. Shown in the reveal only if the learner moved the floor below $6.

claims.text: Baked loaves that buyers do not take at the floor price are a surplus.
claims.source: Standard usage, e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 6 (price floors and surpluses).

claims.text: The lesson is a model: straight lines, one market, bakers bake what they would supply at the floor price; it makes no claim about any real minimum price.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Toy bread market: straight lines'. Real floors often come with buying schemes or quotas that change who holds the surplus.

recall.question: A rule holds a price well above where supply and demand cross. What do you expect to see?
options: More sold, because sellers earn more
A pile of goods made but not bought
recall.why: At the higher price buyers want less and sellers offer more, so the gap between them is left unsold: a surplus.
